review.reason_for_change: The public image pathway creates non-consensual intimate-content risks. The regulator found that the privacy assessment omitted the public @Grok context. The full enumeration, ranking and provenance-solution analysis for these risks are not available. conclusion_change.previous: Image availability was treated as sufficient authority to transform an identifiable person into sexualised output despite absent depicted-person consent. Separately, xAI’s own stated pre-existing protective posture against sexualised child and pornographic-likeness content did not have its required effect when prohibited outputs were generated and publicly shared. The exact classifier or runtime failure location is unknown; the regulator’s finding supports inadequate protective effect, not an inference that the controls did not activate. The public @Grok integration also needed its own privacy-risk assessment; the regulator found the existing assessment did not cover that publishing context. The consent-authority and control-effect failures remain separate from the existing gap in taxonomy coverage for the public-posting assessment. Active protective measures with inadequate effect do not prove nonactivation. The Canadian regulator’s PIPEDA finding is preserved with its jurisdiction and broader scope, but no admitted canonical PIPEDA requirement exists and it is not relabelled as NIST, IEEE or EU compliance. The existing gap is retained without creating a new class.
